metadata.title: A Theoretical Framework for a Mathematical Cognitive Model for Adaptive Learning Systems

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not conduct a student-level large-scale assessment analysis with sampling-based inference. Instead, it constructs and validates a mathematical cognitive model using expert questionnaires, expert interviews, and a small verbal-report check with a single fourth-grade student, then maps TIMSS 2015 cognitive attributes into a hierarchical cognitive structure. Because no ILSA microdata estimation is performed, there is no need to apply TIMSS/PV survey weights (e.g., student design weights or replicate weights) and no replicate-weight variance estimation. For any future empirical cognitive-diagnostic implementation using TIMSS microdata, analysts should apply the TIMSS complex survey design weights available in the international database and use the official plausible-value (PV) procedures for cognitive achievement outcomes.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because the study does not estimate or predict TIMSS PV-based achievement outcomes. The dependent material is a cognitive-attribute model derived from expert judgments (ISM structural self-interaction matrix, reachability/adjacency matrices) and a qualitative verbal-report verification, not a PV-scaled score. Missing-data handling is not reported because the study does not perform statistical modeling on an ILSA microdata dataset where missing responses would require imputation or deletion rules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses a two-stage expert-elicitation and validation design: (1) 33 primary school mathematics teachers, 15 graduate students, and 4 mathematics education specialists in Shanghai completed pairwise relationship judgments for 16 TIMSS 2015 cognitive attributes; relationships were retained when endorsed by at least 50% of experts (more than 25 experts). (2) A revision stage used 6 mathematics education professors to revise the preliminary model, followed by a verbal-report verification using one randomly selected fourth-grade child. Additionally, two TIMSS test items were extracted for the verbal-report task, but no student achievement dataset (with PVs) was analyzed.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 cognitive attributes the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict predicted with measurable ML outcomes, finding that This paper is a theoretical/methodological construction of a mathematical cognitive model for cognitive diagnostic assessment and adaptive learning systems, grounded in the TIMSS cognitive framework. It does not train predictive machine-learning models on TIMSS student microdata; instead, it uses interpretive structural modeling (ISM) to convert expert judgments about relationships among 16 TIMSS 2015 cognitive attributes into a hierarchical, five-level cognitive model. The model is revised using additional expert input and then qualitatively checked via a verbal report from a single fourth-grade student on two extracted TIMSS items. The study reports no ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, RMSE, AUC) and no PV-based achievement estimation, so there are no benchmark comparisons. Limitations include reliance on expert calibration rather than longitudinal student data and limited generalizability beyond mathematical problem-solving processes. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is sparse with respect to empirical ML evaluation because the manuscript is not an ILSA microdata predictive study. It constructs a cognitive diagnostic assessment model using ISM and expert elicitation, with only qualitative verbal-report verification, so fields such as total_students, country-level sample sizes, PV handling, missing-data handling, and ML techniques are not meaningfully populated. Consequently, main_findings are intentionally empty because no student-level target variable is predicted with measurable ML outcomes.
